name: JSON Formatter & Validator
title: JSON Formatter & Validator — Free Online Beautifier
description: Format, minify, validate and sort JSON in your browser. See clear parse errors, choose indentation and copy the result instantly.
intro: Turn dense JSON into readable, consistently indented output, minify it for transport, or check it for syntax errors — all locally in your browser.
instructions: Paste or type a JSON document into the input box.
Choose Format to beautify it or Minify to remove optional whitespace.
Adjust indentation or enable alphabetical key sorting when needed.
Review the status line, then copy or download the result.

faqs.q: Is my JSON uploaded to a server?
faqs.a: No. The JSON is parsed and printed by JavaScript running in your browser. This page does not send your input to LetitEdit or to a third-party formatting service.

Formatting and minifying only change whitespace outside string values, so numbers, booleans and text stay the same. Enabling key sorting does change the order of object properties, but not their values or array order.

faqs.q: Why does the validator reject comments or trailing commas?
faqs.a: Standard JSON does not allow comments or a comma after the final item. The browser parser enforces the JSON specification. JSON5 and JSONC extensions are not accepted unless you remove those features first.

faqs.q: Can it validate against my API schema?
faqs.a: No. This tool checks JSON syntax only. A document can be valid JSON while still having the wrong field names or types. Use a JSON Schema validator when you need to enforce an API contract.
No. Arrays keep their original order because position can be meaningful. Sorting is applied recursively to object keys only.

article.heading: Why formatting JSON makes debugging easier
paragraphs: JSON is deliberately compact. A single API response, configuration export or log entry can arrive as one very long line, which is efficient for machines and miserable for people. A formatter parses that line and prints it again with consistent indentation, line breaks and spacing, so nested objects and arrays become visible at a glance. The data does not change; only its presentation does. That small change makes it much easier to spot a missing field, compare two responses, review a pull request or explain a payload to a colleague. Because the work happens in your browser, you can paste a response while debugging without sending it to a third-party formatting service.

article.heading: What validation checks and what it does not
paragraphs: The formatter validates syntax with the browser's built-in JSON parser. That means it enforces the rules of the JSON specification: keys and strings must use double quotes, commas cannot trail the last item, comments are not allowed, and values must be strings, numbers, true, false, null, objects or arrays. When parsing fails, the page shows the parser's error message so you can find the problem instead of guessing. Validation is not a schema check. A document can be valid JSON while containing the wrong field names, missing required values or an unexpected type. Use a schema validator when you need to enforce a contract, and use this formatter to confirm that the document is syntactically sound.

article.heading: Pretty printing versus minifying
paragraphs: Pretty printing adds whitespace so humans can read the structure. Minifying removes every optional space, tab and newline so the payload is as small as possible. Both modes produce the same data, and switching between them is a useful way to confirm that formatting has not changed the meaning. Minified JSON is common in API requests, configuration bundles and storage where bytes matter. Formatted JSON is better for documentation, reviews and troubleshooting. Whitespace inside string values is always preserved, so minifying will not alter a message, URL or description. If a value contains meaningful leading or trailing spaces, they remain part of the string after either operation.

article.heading: Choosing indentation and sorting keys
paragraphs: You can indent with two spaces, four spaces or a tab. Two spaces are a good default because they keep deeply nested documents narrow enough to read on a laptop. Four spaces are easier to scan when the structure is shallow, while tabs let each editor display the depth it prefers. The optional key-sort control reorders object properties alphabetically and applies the same rule to nested objects. Array order is never changed because arrays often represent sequences where position matters. Sorting is handy for comparing two versions of a configuration file, but avoid it when a downstream system depends on property order. JSON technically treats objects as unordered, yet real code sometimes observes insertion order.

article.heading: A safe everyday workflow
paragraphs: Paste the document into the input box and choose Format. If the output is empty and the status turns red, read the parser message and correct the syntax before continuing. Once the structure looks right, use Minify when you need a compact payload, or keep the formatted version for documentation. Copy or download the result only after reviewing it. Remove passwords, tokens, personal data and internal hostnames before sharing a payload, even when processing is local, because the output may still end up in a ticket or chat message. Very large documents can be slow in any browser, so split enormous exports where possible. For a quick conversion of escaped or encoded content, pair this tool with the Base64 encoder or the regex tester.

name: Base64 Encoder & Decoder
title: Base64 Encoder & Decoder — UTF-8 and URL-Safe
description: Encode text to Base64 or decode Base64 to UTF-8 text. Supports accents, emoji, URL-safe characters and optional padding, entirely in your browser.
placeholder: Type or paste the text you want to encode…
intro: Convert UTF-8 text to Base64 and back again, with URL-safe output and clear errors when a value is not valid Base64 or not valid UTF-8.
instructions: Choose Encode to convert text to Base64, or Decode to convert Base64 back to text.
Paste your input into the box. The result updates as you type.
Enable URL-safe output if the value will appear in a URL or token.
Copy the result, or use the swap button to send it back through the reverse direction.

faqs.q: Is Base64 a form of encryption?
faqs.a: No. Base64 is a reversible text representation of bytes. Anyone with the string can decode it. Never use Base64 to protect passwords, API keys or private records; use proper encryption and key management instead.

faqs.q: Why is the encoded output longer than the input?
faqs.a: Base64 represents every three bytes with four ASCII characters, so the encoded form is about one third larger. UTF-8 text can also use multiple bytes per character, which affects the final length.

faqs.q: Does the tool support Unicode and emoji?
faqs.a: Yes. Text is converted to UTF-8 bytes before encoding, so accented letters, non-Latin scripts and emoji round-trip correctly. Decoding validates that the bytes are valid UTF-8 text.

It replaces plus with a hyphen and slash with an underscore, and usually removes equals-sign padding. This makes the value safer inside URLs, filenames and JSON Web Tokens. The decoder accepts both standard and URL-safe alphabets.

faqs.q: Why do I get an error when decoding?
faqs.a: The value may contain characters outside the Base64 alphabet, have an impossible length, or represent binary data that is not valid UTF-8 text. Check that you copied the complete value and that it is text rather than an image or encrypted file.

controls.label: Use URL-safe characters (- and _) without padding

article.heading: What Base64 encoding actually does
paragraphs: Base64 represents binary data using 64 printable ASCII characters: A–Z, a–z, 0–9, plus and slash. Every three input bytes become four output characters, which is why encoded data is roughly one third larger than the original. The format exists because many systems were designed to carry text and cannot safely transport raw bytes. Email attachments, data URLs, JSON fields and authentication headers all rely on this kind of text-safe representation. An encoder does not interpret the content. It simply maps bytes to characters according to a fixed table, optionally adds padding and returns a string that can travel through text-only channels without being mistaken for control characters.

article.heading: Why UTF-8 matters for accents and emoji
paragraphs: Text is not stored as characters inside a computer; it is stored as bytes. This tool converts your text to UTF-8 first, then encodes those bytes. That detail matters for accented letters, non-Latin scripts and emoji. The word Café contains a two-byte é in UTF-8, and an emoji can occupy four bytes, so their Base64 output will not match a naive character-by-character calculation. When decoding, the tool reverses the process and validates the result as UTF-8. If the bytes are not valid UTF-8 text, it reports an error rather than showing replacement symbols. This strict behaviour helps you notice when you are decoding a file, image or encrypted value instead of text.

article.heading: Standard Base64, URL-safe Base64 and padding
paragraphs: Standard Base64 uses plus and slash, but those characters have special meanings in URLs and can be altered by form handling. URL-safe Base64 replaces plus with a hyphen and slash with an underscore, making the result safer to place in a query string or filename. Padding uses equals signs to fill the final group to four characters. Some systems keep the padding; others strip it. This decoder accepts both alphabets and can restore missing padding automatically, so you can paste a value copied from a JWT, a data URL or an API response without editing it first. The encoder's URL-safe option removes padding as well, matching the common token convention.

article.heading: Common practical uses
paragraphs: Base64 appears in more places than many developers expect. Data URLs embed small images, fonts and icons directly in CSS or HTML. Email uses MIME encoding for attachments. JSON APIs sometimes carry binary blobs as strings. JWTs encode their header and payload segments with URL-safe Base64, although the result is not encrypted. Basic authentication headers combine a username and password with Base64. Log files and debugging tools may show encoded values that need a quick decode. A browser-based encoder is convenient for these checks because it needs no install and leaves nothing on a server. For round-trip work, use the swap button to send the output back through the opposite direction.

article.heading: What Base64 is not
paragraphs: Base64 is not encryption, compression or a security control. Anyone who has the string can decode it with a few lines of code, so it must never be used to hide passwords, API keys or private records. It also adds size rather than reducing it. If you need to protect data, use encryption and key management designed for that purpose. If you need to shrink data, use compression. Use Base64 only when a text-only channel requires a safe representation of bytes. Remember that clipboard history, browser extensions and shared screens can expose anything you paste, even though this tool processes locally. Decode only data you trust, and validate the result before feeding it into another system.

name: Regex Tester & Match Highlighter
title: Regex Tester — Test JavaScript Regular Expressions
description: Test JavaScript regular expressions against sample text. See highlighted matches, capture groups, flags and replacement output instantly in your browser.
placeholder: Paste the text you want to test…
intro: Write a JavaScript regular expression, choose flags and see every match highlighted, with capture groups and an optional replacement preview.
instructions: Enter a regular expression and choose the flags you need.
Paste a representative test string into the input box.
Review the highlighted matches and the table of groups and indexes.
Add replacement text to preview the result, then copy what you need.

faqs.q: Which regular expression flavour does this tool use?
faqs.a: It uses the JavaScript engine in your browser, the same one used by new RegExp() and String.replace(). Patterns written for PCRE, Python or Java may need changes, especially around named groups, inline flags and some escape sequences.

faqs.q: What does the global flag change?
faqs.a: Without the global flag the tester stops after the first match. With it enabled, every match is highlighted and listed, up to a safety limit of 1,000 results.
Yes. Numbered and named groups appear in the match table. Optional groups that did not participate are shown as empty, and each match includes its starting index in the original test string.

faqs.q: Does the replacement preview modify my text?
faqs.a: No. The replacement is calculated for preview only. Nothing is changed until you copy the output or apply the pattern in your own code.

faqs.q: Can I use lookbehind or Unicode property escapes?
faqs.a: Lookbehind and property escapes such as \p{Letter} are supported in current browsers but may be unavailable in older ones. Enable the Unicode flag for property escapes. The tester reports an error if the engine cannot compile the pattern.

article.heading: What a JavaScript regex tester does
paragraphs: A regular expression is a compact pattern language for finding, validating and replacing text. This tester runs patterns with the JavaScript regular-expression engine in your browser, so the behaviour you see matches what new RegExp() and String.replace() do in web code. That distinction matters: JavaScript regex is not identical to PCRE, Python's re module or Java's Pattern class. Some constructs behave differently and some advanced features are unavailable. Testing here helps you confirm flags, escaping and capture groups before shipping a pattern to production. Paste a representative sample, adjust the pattern, and watch the highlighted matches and match table update. No text or pattern is sent to a server.

article.heading: How flags change the result
paragraphs: Flags modify how the engine interprets a pattern. Global searches every match instead of stopping at the first one. Ignore case makes letters match regardless of case. Multiline changes the meaning of the start and end anchors so they apply to each line. Dot-all lets a period match line breaks. Unicode enables code-point-aware behaviour and is required for property escapes such as \p{Letter}. The tester shows the effective flags next to the match count, so you can see exactly what is active. If a pattern works in one language but not another, compare the flags first; a missing global flag or an unexpected multiline anchor is a common reason for different results.

article.heading: Capture groups, indexes and named groups
paragraphs: Parentheses create capture groups. The match table lists each group's value alongside the overall match and its starting index, which makes it easier to debug extraction patterns. Named groups, written as (?<name>...), appear by name instead of by number and are usually easier to maintain. Numbering follows the order of opening parentheses, including nested groups. Non-capturing groups (?:...) group without adding an entry. If a group is optional and did not participate in the match, it is shown as empty rather than as the text undefined. Start indexes refer to the original test string, not to the highlighted preview. Zero-length matches are marked with a symbol because they select a position rather than a span of characters.

article.heading: Testing replacements before you apply them
paragraphs: When you enter replacement text, the tester runs the same flags through JavaScript's replace operation and shows the result below the match list. Replacement syntax supports $1, $2 and so on for numbered groups, $<name> for named groups, $& for the whole match and $$ for a literal dollar sign. The preview is useful for tasks such as reformatting dates, swapping name order or wrapping values in quotes. It also exposes mistakes quickly: a reference to a group that does not exist stays literal, and an unexpected global flag may replace more text than intended. Review the replacement preview and the match table before copying the output into source code or a data migration script.

article.heading: Writing patterns that stay readable and safe
paragraphs: Start with the smallest pattern that matches your sample, then add one constraint at a time. Use anchors when the whole string must match, character classes for allowed characters, and explicit escaping for punctuation such as dots and question marks. Test empty input, punctuation, Unicode text and very long strings. Avoid nested quantifiers that can cause catastrophic backtracking on hostile input. In JavaScript, prefer simple string checks when a regex is not necessary, and cap the amount of text you process. Keep patterns in named constants with a comment explaining the intent. This tester highlights matches and caps results at one thousand, but it does not make an unsafe pattern safe in production.
